To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) HLC monitoring can augment electrophoretics in multiple myelomas achieving VGPR and (2) HLC responses might be prognostic, partly depending on the ability to recover normal HLC ratios.

(1) HLC responses are associated with clinical outcome in patients achieving VGPr, (2) HLC-pair suppressions are associated with inferior clinical outcome and (3) abnormal HLC ratios have better concordance than immunofixation with multiparametric FCM for detecting clonal disease in the bone marrow of patients achieving VGPR.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new assay for the monitoring of patients with multiple myeloma, and the clinical significance of these results.
the clinical impact of HLC responses in newly diagnosed patients.
the development of a novel assay for monitoring the immune status of patients with multiple myeloma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HLC assay is a more sensitive tool to detect and monitor minimal residual disease than the electrophoresis method.
the HLC ratio is a more accurate method to determine response to treatment in MM patients.

HLC response monitoring is an important tool in multiple myelomas, which is complementary to the traditional M-spike assessment and can be used in the future to improve the management of patients with multiple myeloma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

HLC monitoring can be used to identify patients with a higher risk of progression, and that HLC-pair analysis could help to stratify these patients further into those with an increased risk of relapse.
HLC measurements are a useful adjunct to the current standard of care for response assessment in multiple myelomas.
HLC-pair ratio monitoring could be used to improve the accuracy of the response assessment in patients with multiple myeloma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HLC responses are a useful tool for risk stratification of myeloma patients, and can be used in conjunction with flow cytometry to better define the extent of disease.
HLC monitoring is an important prognostic tool in multiple myelomas.

HLC monitoring can provide additional information on the response to anti-myeloma treatment, which may be important for clinical decision-making and for improving our understanding of the biology and pathophysiology of multiple myeloma.
